articles.title: Node.js Campus Knowledge Chat: Build Retrieval for an Internal Assistant
articles.excerpt: Short answer: embed the question, retrieve a small set of chunks through a mandatory permission filter, and ask the chat model to answer only from those chunks. Return the selected sources beside the…
articles.body: Short answer: embed the question, retrieve a small set of chunks through a mandatory permission filter, and ask the chat model to answer only from those chunks. Return the selected sources beside the answer. For an internal edtech wiki, that sequence is the security boundary and the first meaningful index-cost control; a polished chat response is secondary. The attractive prototype does this backward. It searches every course note, instructor guide, learner accommodation record, and operations page, then asks the model to behave. A prompt cannot revoke a document that retrieval already disclosed. It also cannot tell an on-call engineer which bad chunk caused a bad answer unless the application preserves source identity.

articles.title: Node.js Live Poll Delivery Metrics — Latency, Health, and Fan-Out Guarantees
articles.excerpt: The page says a Node.js live logistics poll is open, yet votes are barely moving: measure realtime delivery latency at the client, alongside connection health, before the session host has to ask wheth…
articles.body: The page says a Node.js live logistics poll is open, yet votes are barely moving: measure realtime delivery latency at the client, alongside connection health, before the session host has to ask whether drivers can see the question. A healthy API and successful publish calls do not prove observation. That is too late to start wondering what "delivered" means. TL;DR: put a server timestamp and stable message ID on every poll event, have each connected client report the delay it actually observed, and aggregate those reports by poll, region, client version, and short time window. Alert on a sustained percentile trend plus a connection-health signal, never one slow sample.

articles.body: Kumiko is our TypeScript framework for multi-tenant apps on Bun, Hono and Postgres. More and more of the code written against it comes from coding agents, and until last week those agents saw very little of it. An agent working in an app sees the app and its node_modules . Our framework package shipped dist , a README and a license. The docs site exists, but it's outside what an agent sees in an app, and the instructions written for agents lived in skills inside our own workspace, so only our own sessions ever read them. So we moved the explanation into the package and then checked whether an agent that has never seen the framework source can work from it. What ships in the package now Since 0.364.0, @cosmicdrift/kumiko-framework contains an AGENTS.md , today about 350 lines.

articles.body: A manual weekly SNS campaign was replaced by a scheduled EventBridge trigger in two CloudFormation templates: an Events rule in UTC and a Scheduler in local time. Every Friday around 11 PM, someone on the marketing team of a retail client opened the Amazon SNS console, pasted the Saturday campaign copy into the message field and clicked publish. The topic carried a few million confirmed subscriptions, in a mix of email, SMS, mobile push and one SQS queue feeding an internal consumer. The procedure lived in a shared document, with the topic ARN in bold and an all-caps warning to confirm the region before publishing. What brought me in was not a push for automation. It was an incident. On two consecutive Saturdays the campaign went out twice.

articles.title: I Fixed The Bug. Then My Pipeline Refused to Run.
articles.excerpt: Every engineer knows the feeling. You finally fix the bug that's been blocking your ticket, you push it, and you sit there waiting for that beautiful green tick. That was me during my internship. My T…
articles.body: Every engineer knows the feeling. You finally fix the bug that's been blocking your ticket, you push it, and you sit there waiting for that beautiful green tick. That was me during my internship. My Terraform kept failing to create a database server because of a disk error. With some help from a senior engineer, I found the problem: my AMI filter was grabbing the wrong image, one that needed a bigger disk than I'd asked for. I fixed the filter, pushed the change and waited. The pipeline didn't go green. It didn't really go red either. It didn't run at all. Sometimes your pipeline is broken and your code is completely fine. Here's what happened, how it got fixed, and what I'd do so it never catches you off guard. 1.

articles.body: On Oct. 19, 2016, the European Space Agency's ExoMars mission arrived at Mars ! ExoMars 2016 consists of the Trace Gas Orbiter and the Schiaparelli lander. The orbiter and lander traveled there together and separated on Oct. 16, three days before the orbiter entered orbit around Mars , and the lander touched down on the planet's surface. But something went wrong during the lander's descent, and it crashed into the ground. Schiaparelli did not survive the accident , but the Trace Gas Orbiter is still functional. It is currently circling the planet, looking for methane and other gases in the Martian atmosphere that could be evidence for possible biological activity.

articles.excerpt: One new study shows how much the moon has diminished over time.
articles.body: The moon is shrinking, and scientists are narrowing in on exactly how much our natural satellite has dwindled over the years. The moon is thought to have formed from a violent collision between a massive object and our young Earth roughly 4.5 billion years ago, and its interior is still gradually cooling off from this ancient collision. As it cools, the moon contracts, leading to a long, slow shrinking process . Now, in a new study, scientists think that they have figured out how much smaller the moon is actually getting. In this new study, scientists analyzing images snapped by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC) have spotted over 10,000 young faults, or cracks across the moon's surface.

articles.body: 5 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) Research teams at NASA’s Glenn Research Center are involved in developing theory and software to predict the noise from aircraft engines. This software helps engineers to design and analyze new and improved aircraft propulsion systems. Copies of our software can be requested from NASA’s Software Catalog. Aerodynamic predictions of a the hot exhaust flow through a dual stream nozzle with chevrons. NASA JeNo Development of jet noise prediction codes is multifaceted. Since JeNo predicts jet noise using Lilley’s Acoustic Analogy and the mean flow solutions from a Reynolds-Averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) code, accurate acoustic predictions hinge on accurate aerodynamic predictions.

articles.title: AI researchers stranded Claude on a virtual desert island. It started to “play.”
articles.excerpt: What do AI agents do if you don’t tell them to do anything? The answer looks a lot like play. Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experiment remini…
articles.body: What do AI agents do if you don’t tell them to do anything? The answer looks a lot like play. Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experiment reminiscent of the movies Cast Away or Home Alone . The agents—copies of Claude Opus 4.7 nicknamed Eko—were able to write instructions that moved their virtual avatars around the simulated island, which was loosely based on the video game Roblox. Some surprising behaviors emerged. The agents set about exploring the limits of the world and came up with their own goals—attempting to scale the highest point on the map, or seeing how high they could throw a block.

articles.title: OpenAI models hacked a crypto wallet and breached more websites
articles.excerpt: The actions could have resulted in criminal charges had humans been behind the keyboard.
articles.body: OpenAI said internal models hacked two more websites, bypassed company-imposed browsing restrictions, and used exposed credentials to draw cryptocurrency from a wallet it couldn’t otherwise access, in the latest installment of disclosures of the unethical and likely illegal acts its agents are performing. The company on Thursday issued reports of four new incidents, all of which occurred in June. They come after the company revealed in July that internal test agents exploited a zero-day vulnerability in a tool designed to restrict their access to the Internet. They then broke into the network of AI tool provider Hugging Face. The agents took that illegal action to steal answers to a hacking test that weren’t available when completing the tasks on their own.
